description: Production networking troubleshooting runbook focused on the commands that resolve 90% of day-to-day connectivity, DNS, TLS, and proxy incidents.

commands.title: Show listening sockets and owning processes
commands.summary: Lists all TCP and UDP listening sockets together with the process that owns them.
commands.problem: Connection refused, port already in use, or a service that claims to be running but is not accepting traffic.
commands.why_this_command: Fastest authoritative view of what is actually bound on the host. Replaces the older netstat in modern distributions.
thinking_process: Users report connection refused or a port conflict.
ss -tulnp shows every listening port and the PID/program.
I immediately know whether the expected process is listening and on which address.
commands.expected_output: Netid State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port Process
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Look at Local Address:Port. 0.0.0.0 or * means all interfaces; 127.0.0.1 means localhost only. The Process column gives the binary and PID. Absence of the expected port means the service is not listening.
real_world_incidents: Service bound only to 127.0.0.1 while traffic arrived on the public interface.
Two processes fighting for the same port after a failed deploy.
Old process still holding the port after a crash.
common_mistakes: Running without root/capabilities and missing the process name.
Looking only at TCP and missing a UDP service.
Misreading 127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0.
what_to_check_before: Run as root or with CAP_NET_ADMIN to see process names.
what_to_check_after: If the port is missing → check service status and logs.
If the wrong process owns it → stop that process and restart the correct one.
Confirm with curl or nc from another host.
best_practices: ss -tulnp is the first command for any 'port in use' or 'connection refused' incident.
Always verify both the port and the bind address.
commands.interview_question: A service is running according to systemctl but clients get connection refused. What do you check first?
commands.interview_answer: ss -tulnp to confirm the process is actually listening and on which address. It is common for a service to be running yet bound only to localhost or a different port.

commands.title: Test HTTP/HTTPS endpoint reachability and response
commands.summary: Performs HTTP requests and surfaces status codes, headers, TLS errors, and body content.
commands.problem: Is the service reachable? What status does it return? Is TLS broken? Is a proxy or load balancer interfering?
commands.why_this_command: The universal tool for validating application-layer connectivity from the command line. Works for health checks, upstreams, and external endpoints.
thinking_process: Monitoring or users report errors.
curl -v or curl -I from the same network namespace shows the real response.
I can distinguish connection refused, TLS problems, 5xx, and timeouts.
commands.expected_output: HTTP status line, headers, and optionally the body or a numeric status code
commands.how_to_interpret_output: First look at the status code. Connection refused or timeout means lower-layer failure. SSL errors point to certificate or SNI issues. 5xx means the application or upstream is broken.
real_world_incidents: Health-check endpoint returning 500 after a config change.
TLS handshake failure caused by an expired certificate.
Service listening only on localhost while curl was aimed at the public IP.
common_mistakes: Using -k in production scripts and hiding real certificate problems.
Not following redirects when the endpoint requires -L.
Testing from the wrong network namespace (host vs container vs pod).
what_to_check_before: Know the expected URL, scheme, and whether TLS is required.
what_to_check_after: Connection refused → ss -tulnp
TLS error → check certificate expiry and chain
5xx → application or reverse-proxy logs
best_practices: Prefer curl -v for interactive debugging and the -w format string for scripting.
Always test from the same place the real client traffic originates when possible.
commands.interview_question: How do you retrieve only the HTTP status code of an endpoint without printing the body?

commands.title: Resolve DNS names with detailed output
commands.summary: Queries DNS and displays the full answer, authority, and the server that responded.
commands.problem: DNS resolution failed, returned the wrong IP, or is timing out. Applications cannot reach dependencies by name.
commands.why_this_command: More informative and scriptable than nslookup or host. Shows exactly what the resolver returned and which server answered.
thinking_process: Application logs show 'name or service not known' or connect to an unexpected IP.
dig tells me whether resolution succeeds, what IP is returned, and which nameserver answered.
I can also query a specific server to isolate the fault.
commands.expected_output: QUESTION, ANSWER, AUTHORITY sections plus the SERVER line at the bottom
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Empty ANSWER or SERVFAIL means resolution failure. Compare the returned IP with the expected value. The SERVER line shows which resolver answered; this helps distinguish local vs upstream problems.
real_world_incidents: Stale DNS cache pointing at a decommissioned load balancer.
CoreDNS or internal DNS outage causing widespread service discovery failure.
Split-horizon DNS returning different answers inside versus outside the VPC.
common_mistakes: Not checking /etc/hosts which overrides DNS.
Querying only the local resolver and missing that the upstream is broken.
Ignoring TTL and caching behaviour.
what_to_check_after: If local resolution fails but public DNS works → check the local resolver or network path to it.
If the wrong IP is returned → examine the zone data or intermediate caches.
best_practices: Use dig +short for quick IP lookups and full dig for diagnosis.
Always test both the application nameserver and a known-good public resolver.
commands.interview_question: How do you determine which DNS server answered a query and what IP was returned?
commands.interview_answer: Run dig hostname. The ANSWER section contains the IP and the SERVER line at the bottom shows the resolver that responded.

commands.title: Test basic IP reachability
commands.summary: Sends ICMP echo requests to verify host reachability and measure round-trip time.
commands.problem: Is the remote host up? Is there basic IP connectivity before debugging ports or applications?
commands.why_this_command: Quickest way to rule out complete network isolation or a down host before moving to TCP or application layers.
thinking_process: A service is unreachable.
Before looking at ports or TLS I confirm the host answers ping.
If ping fails the problem is routing, firewall, or the host itself.
commands.expected_output: Reply lines with RTT or 100% packet loss summary
commands.how_to_interpret_output: 0% loss and low RTT means basic connectivity is present. 100% loss means the host is down, unreachable, or ICMP is blocked. High latency or jitter points to network congestion or a poor path.
real_world_incidents: Host became unreachable after a route-table or security-group change.
Intermittent packet loss causing application timeouts.
DNS resolved correctly but the IP was black-holed.
common_mistakes: Assuming ping failure always means the host is down (ICMP is frequently blocked).
Letting ping run forever instead of using -c.
Pinging a name without first verifying DNS.
what_to_check_before: Prefer an IP address when testing pure connectivity so DNS is not a confounding factor.
what_to_check_after: Ping works but TCP fails → check listening ports and firewalls with ss and curl.
Ping fails → traceroute/mtr or inspect security groups / iptables / routes.
best_practices: Always limit the number of packets with -c in shared terminals and scripts.
Remember that many cloud security groups and corporate firewalls drop ICMP.
commands.interview_question: Ping succeeds but a TCP connection to port 80 fails. What are the most likely causes?
commands.interview_answer: Nothing is listening on port 80, a firewall is blocking TCP/80, or the service is bound only to localhost.

commands.title: Inspect TLS certificate and handshake
commands.summary: Performs a TLS handshake and prints the certificate chain, validity dates, and negotiated parameters.
commands.problem: TLS errors, expired certificates, incomplete chains, or SNI mismatches causing connection failures.
commands.why_this_command: The definitive low-level tool for diagnosing certificate and handshake problems that curl may only surface as a generic SSL error.
thinking_process: curl or a browser reports a certificate problem.
openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host shows the exact chain and dates.
I can see whether the cert is expired, the chain is incomplete, or the wrong certificate is being served.
examples: echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates
commands.expected_output: Certificate chain, subject, issuer, validity dates, and Verify return code
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Verify return code 0 means success. Non-zero indicates the problem (expired, self-signed, unable to get local issuer, etc.). Check notBefore/notAfter for expiry. Confirm the subject matches the expected hostname.
real_world_incidents: Certificate expired at midnight and broke all HTTPS traffic.
Incomplete chain because the intermediate certificate was missing from the server config.
SNI mismatch after a new virtual host was added.
common_mistakes: Omitting -servername and receiving the default certificate instead of the name-based one.
Not piping a quit or using </dev/null and leaving the session open.
Looking only at the leaf certificate and missing chain issues.
what_to_check_before: Know the exact hostname and port the client is connecting to.
what_to_check_after: Expired → renew and reload the service.
Incomplete chain → install the missing intermediate.
Wrong certificate → fix the virtual-host or load-balancer configuration.
best_practices: Always supply -servername for name-based virtual hosts.
Automate expiry checks; never rely on manual discovery during an outage.
commands.interview_question: How do you check the expiry date of the certificate presented by a remote HTTPS service?
commands.interview_answer: echo | openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates

commands.title: Trace the network path to a destination
commands.summary: Shows the sequence of routers (hops) between the local host and a destination together with per-hop latency.
commands.problem: Traffic is slow, intermittently lost, or reaches the wrong place. Where is the path breaking or degrading?
commands.why_this_command: Reveals routing problems, black holes, and high-latency hops that ping alone cannot surface.
thinking_process: Ping shows high latency or loss, or a service is reachable from some networks but not others.
traceroute maps the path and highlights the hop where problems begin.
I can then focus investigation on that network segment or provider.
commands.expected_output: Numbered list of hops with IP addresses and three RTT samples each
commands.how_to_interpret_output: Look for the first hop that shows * * * (no response) or a sudden jump in latency. That hop or the link to it is usually the problem. Consistent high latency from a certain hop onward indicates congestion or a suboptimal route.
real_world_incidents: Traffic taking a suboptimal path after a BGP change.
Packet loss starting at a specific ISP hop.
Internal routing loop visible as repeating addresses.
common_mistakes: Assuming every * means a hard failure (many routers simply do not respond to the probe type).
Not using -n and waiting for reverse DNS on every hop.
Using only UDP probes when a firewall blocks them; TCP probes (-T) are often more reliable.
what_to_check_before: Confirm basic connectivity with ping if possible.
what_to_check_after: If the path breaks inside your network → check routes, firewalls, and security groups.
If the path breaks outside → escalate to the network team or provider with the traceroute output.
best_practices: Prefer mtr when available for a continuous, statistical view.
Capture traceroute output in incident notes; it is often requested by network teams.
commands.interview_question: Traceroute shows successful hops up to hop 8 and then all asterisks. What does that usually indicate?
commands.interview_answer: Either the destination or an intermediate router is dropping the probe packets (common with ICMP/UDP rate limiting or firewalls), or there is a black hole starting at that hop. Further testing with TCP probes or from another source is needed.

commands.title: Display and manipulate the routing table
commands.summary: Shows the kernel routing table and allows inspection of how packets will leave the host for a given destination.
commands.problem: Traffic is going out the wrong interface, a route is missing, or a host cannot reach a subnet that should be reachable.
commands.why_this_command: Authoritative view of the routes the kernel is actually using. Essential when debugging multi-homed hosts, VPCs, or policy routing.
thinking_process: Packets are not reaching the expected next hop or are leaving via the wrong NIC.
ip route show gives the full table; ip route get <dst> shows the exact route that will be used.
I can confirm whether a required route exists and is correct.
commands.syntax: ip route [show] | ip route get ADDRESS
commands.expected_output: destination via gateway dev interface src ... or default via ...
commands.how_to_interpret_output: The default route is the most important for general internet access. For a specific destination, ip route get shows the exact path the kernel will take, including the source address and device. Missing or incorrect routes explain many 'no route to host' errors.
real_world_incidents: Missing route to a peered VPC after a Terraform apply.
Traffic leaving via the wrong interface on a multi-homed bastion.
Default route pointing at a dead gateway after a network change.
common_mistakes: Looking only at the default route and missing more specific routes that take precedence.
Confusing the routing table with firewall rules.
Not checking policy routing tables when multiple tables are in use.
what_to_check_before: Know the destination IP or subnet that is failing.
what_to_check_after: If a route is missing → add it (or fix the configuration management that should have added it).
If the route looks correct → move on to firewalls, security groups, or the next hop itself.
best_practices: Use ip route get <dst> for a definitive answer on how a packet will be routed.
Prefer configuration management or cloud route tables over permanent manual ip route add commands.
commands.interview_question: How do you determine which interface and gateway a packet to 10.20.30.40 will use?
commands.interview_answer: ip route get 10.20.30.40. The output shows the device, gateway, and source address the kernel will use.

commands.title: Show network interfaces and addresses
commands.summary: Lists network interfaces, their state, MAC addresses, and assigned IPv4/IPv6 addresses.
commands.problem: Is the interface up? Does it have the expected IP? Is there an address conflict or missing secondary IP?
commands.why_this_command: Fundamental view of the host's network identity. Required before almost any deeper network diagnosis.
thinking_process: A host is unreachable or appears to have the wrong IP.
ip addr shows every interface, whether it is UP, and the addresses assigned to it.
I can confirm the host has the IP that DNS and load balancers expect.
commands.expected_output: Interface index, name, state, MTU, MAC, inet/inet6 addresses with scopes
commands.how_to_interpret_output: State UP and LOWER_UP means the interface is administratively and physically up. Confirm the inet address matches expectations. Secondary addresses and IPv6 are also visible. A missing or wrong address explains many connectivity failures.
real_world_incidents: Interface left in DOWN state after a cloud metadata or udev problem.
Missing secondary IP that a service was configured to bind to.
IP address conflict detected after a clone or snapshot restore.
common_mistakes: Looking only at eth0 and missing that the address is on a different interface or alias.
Ignoring the interface state (DOWN vs UP).
Not noticing that an address is tentative or has a short lifetime (DHCP).
what_to_check_after: If the interface is DOWN → bring it up or fix the underlying cloud/network config.
If the address is wrong or missing → correct it via the cloud console, DHCP, or netplan/networkd.
Then re-test with ping and ss.
best_practices: Use ip -br addr for a compact overview during incidents.
Always verify both IPv4 and IPv6 when dual-stack is in use.
commands.interview_question: How do you quickly see all IP addresses assigned to a host in a compact format?
commands.interview_answer: ip -br addr or ip addr show
